# TCP vs UDP

## TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
- **Connection-oriented**: Requires a handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) before data transfer
- **Reliable**: Guarantees delivery; lost packets are retransmitted
- **Ordered**: Data arrives in the order it was sent
- **Flow & congestion control**: Adjusts transmission speed to avoid overwhelming the receiver or network
- **Higher overhead**: Larger headers (20+ bytes) and more latency
- **Stateful**: Both ends maintain connection state

## UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
- **Connectionless**: No handshake; just send datagrams
- **Unreliable**: No guarantee of delivery, ordering, or duplicate protection
- **Fast & lightweight**: Minimal overhead (8-byte header), low latency
- **No congestion control**: Sends at whatever rate the application chooses
- **Stateless**: No connection to maintain

## When to Use Each

| Use Case | Protocol |
|----------|----------|
| Web browsing (HTTP/HTTPS) | TCP |
| Email (SMTP) | TCP |
| File transfer (FTP) | TCP |
| Video streaming / VoIP | UDP |
| Online gaming | UDP |
| DNS lookups | UDP |
| QUIC (modern HTTP/3) | UDP-based, adds reliability on top |

## Key Takeaway
**TCP** trades speed for reliability and order — ideal when all data must arrive intact. **UDP** trades reliability for speed and simplicity — ideal when timeliness matters more than completeness (a dropped video frame is better than a delayed one).

Interestingly, modern protocols like **QUIC** build TCP-like reliability on top of UDP, getting the best of both worlds.
